categories.label: Automated Payment and Performance Verification Mechanisms
categories.memo: Covers how smart contracts operationalize progress payments, incentive/penalty enforcement, and performance verification in prefabricated/modular construction, replacing or supplementing manual administration.

codes.label: Automated Progress Payments
codes.description: Smart contracts trigger payments automatically upon verified conditions (e.g., detected progress, milestones), reducing manual tracking and administrative burden.

sub_codes.label: Condition-Based Triggering
sub_codes.description: Payments are released via 'if/when, then' logic tied to verified events such as detected progress or milestone completion.

sub_codes.label: Three-Stage Payment Frameworks
sub_codes.description: Structured frameworks (preparation, initialization, execution) automate progress payments including digital identities, billing plans, and confirmation/rejection logic.

codes.label: Real-Time Incentive/Penalty Enforcement
codes.description: Smart contracts enforce rewards and penalties continuously throughout the project based on real-time performance data, rather than only at/near completion as in traditional contracts.

codes.label: Objective, Data-Driven Performance Appraisal
codes.description: Replacing subjective, qualitative subcontractor/supplier performance evaluation with objective, instant, quantifiable feedback derived from sensor data, images, or simulation.

codes.label: Fair Reward/Risk Allocation via Cooperative Game Theory
codes.description: Use of Shapley value and other cooperative game-theoretic methods to determine equitable reward/penalty sharing rules among fabricator, equipment provider, labor, and other parties based on marginal contribution.

codes.label: Post-Completion Obligations Automation
codes.description: Extending smart contract logic beyond progress payments to post-completion duties such as defects liability period management and long-term asset maintenance.

categories.label: Blockchain Infrastructure and Oracles
categories.memo: Addresses the technical architecture underpinning smart contracts, including data input mechanisms, verification, and governance structures needed for automated contract administration.

codes.label: Oracles and Evidence Verification
codes.description: Non-deterministic smart contracts rely on external data sources (IoT sensors, images, human-verified inputs) to trigger execution, linking physical performance to contractual conditions.

codes.label: Degree of Decentralization
codes.description: Current blockchain/smart contract implementations remain only partially decentralized, as data inputs typically still require manual verification and entry by a general contractor or central authority.

codes.label: Private vs Public Blockchain Choice
codes.description: Private, permissioned blockchains restricting participation to known parties are considered better suited to construction contracting than public blockchains, due to control over bad actors and data privacy.

codes.label: Immutability Trade-offs
codes.description: Blockchain immutability prevents manipulation of progress/payment data but also prevents correction of erroneous entries, creating governance challenges for fairness and dispute prevention.

categories.label: Limitations and Governance Gaps of Smart Contracts
categories.memo: Captures the persistent technical, legal, and governance limitations that constrain full automation of contract administration via smart contracts in MMC/prefabrication contexts.

codes.label: Inability to Handle Unforeseen Events
codes.description: Smart contracts' rigid, predetermined logic cannot adapt to unexpected circumstances, complex dynamic environments, or change orders, limiting their standalone contractual capability.

codes.label: Need for Human Oversight and Hybrid Governance
codes.description: Automated execution still requires human verification, approval, or pairing with traditional legal contracts to ensure enforceability and handle exceptions.

codes.label: Lack of Mature Governance Models
codes.description: Absence of consistent governance frameworks specifying rights, obligations, and sanctions for noncompliance is a primary barrier to smart contract deployment in construction.

codes.label: Legal and Regulatory Uncertainty
codes.description: Legal enforceability, regulatory treatment of smart contract wallets/execution, and interoperability with existing contract law remain unresolved, creating a gap between technology and contract law.

codes.label: Design and Implementation Risk
codes.description: Poorly designed smart contracts (coding errors, inadequate consensus rules) carry real financial risk, including irreversible losses, underscoring the need for careful adaptive design.

codes.label: Limited Scope of Current Implementations
codes.description: Existing smart contract systems address only narrow aspects of construction administration (e.g., single delivery system, schedule/workforce only), leaving quality compliance, disputes, and multiple constraint types unaddressed.

codes.label: Single Point of Failure in Centralized Data Sources
codes.description: Reliance on a single trusted central database for triggering smart contract execution reintroduces centralization risk, undermining the decentralization rationale.

categories.label: Prefabrication-Specific Coordination and Risk Factors Modeled by Smart Contracts
categories.memo: Focuses on the specific production, logistics, and delivery risks unique to modular/prefabricated construction that smart contract systems are designed to capture and manage.

codes.label: Delivery Sequencing and Variability Risk
codes.description: Out-of-sequence or delayed arrival of prefabricated components disrupts installation balance and project schedule, requiring contractual mechanisms to allocate this risk.

codes.label: Multi-Party Coordination Constraints
codes.description: Coordination among fabricator, logistics/crane providers, and on-site installers creates bottlenecks that smart contracts attempt to proactively manage through make-ready planning.

codes.label: Environmental and External Risk Allocation
codes.description: External conditions such as weather affect bottleneck responsibility and project duration, implying contracts should account for variable environmental risk in prefabricated projects.

codes.label: Simulation-Derived Contractual Benchmarks
codes.description: Simulation modeling (e.g., STROBOSCOPE) generates objective performance benchmarks and scenario-based rules that can be embedded into smart contract incentive/penalty structures.

categories.label: Relational and Financial Context for Smart Contract Adoption
categories.memo: Situates smart contract mechanisms within broader relational contracting and cash flow challenges specific to modular/offsite construction supply chains.

codes.label: Cash Flow Incompatibility in Fragmented Supply Chains
codes.description: Conventional cash flow and payment systems are poorly suited to the fragmented, capital-intensive supply chains of modular/offsite construction, creating financial risk for stakeholders.

codes.label: Reducing Reliance on Third-Party Administration
codes.description: Blockchain-enabled smart contracts reduce dependence on administrators, lawyers, and centralized project managers for payment enforcement, lowering costs and potential disputes.

codes.label: Relational Contracting as Complement to Automation
codes.description: Relational approaches like IPD embed shared risk/reward ('pain-share, gain-share') principles that parallel and can inform smart contract incentive design, though fair early-stage allocation remains challenging.
